title: What ‘Optimizing Search and Siri’ Means in iOS 27 and How to Speed It Up
snippet: Your iPhone will still work, but the process may take some time.
fullText:
If you’ve updated your iPhone to iOS 27, don’t be alarmed if you see a message that reads “Optimizing Search and Siri” in Settings. The message means iOS is rebuilding its search index, a necessary process after this major iOS update because the update implements a brand-new search infrastructure, and the system cannot simply update your existing index. It must crawl through your entire storage drive from scratch.

You can download iOS 27 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

At June’s Worldwide Developers Conference, Apple announced that it was rebuilding its Search interface for iOS 27. The company said the restructure would make searching across your device faster, more reliable and more accurate. In order to do that, iOS 27 has to reindex items across your iPhone. So after you update, you’ll see a banner in Settings that reads “Optimizing Search and Siri.” This is a normal part of the update, and it could take a while to finish, but the good news is you can still use your iPhone during this process.

Here’s what you need to know about the indexing and optimization process once you download iOS 27.

What is indexing?

Data indexing is the process of scanning and organizing metadata from data assets into an index so it can be easily searched.

“Think of it like the index of a book,” data management company Komprise wrote online. “[The index] doesn’t hold the content, but it tells you where to find it, and what’s inside.”

Apple’s support page about Spotlight indexing says that Spotlight search indexes your iPhone when you first set up your device, as data changes on your device and after you update your iPhone. So your device has reindexed before and you likely never noticed – I know I didn’t.

Apple also notes that your iPhone’s index “stays on your device and isn’t shared with Apple or your other devices.” 

Indexing can take hours or days

You can still use your iPhone, even when it’s indexing.LuckyDuck via Getty Images

Apple’s support page notes that indexing could take anywhere from a couple hours to a few days. When I updated my iPhone to a beta version of iOS 27, my iPhone took a couple hours to index, but the more stuff you have stored on your phone, the longer it will take. 

The process takes longer this time around because Apple rebuilt its Search interface in iOS 27. So the update isn’t just adding a few more things to the index, it’s implementing a new search system. 

That means the system isn’t just crawling through the new stuff — it needs to go back through all the data in your phone. Think of it like cataloging new items you’ve bought versus creating an inventory of everything in your home.

Apple does offer a few suggestions on how to speed up the process:

Plug your device into a power source.

Connect your device to Wi-Fi.

Don’t use your iPhone.

OK, can I still use my iPhone?

You can! Indexing doesn’t prevent you from using your iPhone, but it goes faster if you set the phone aside.

If you do use your iPhone during the process, your Spotlight search results might be incomplete because it hasn’t finished indexing. Otherwise, your device should operate as usual. Which is good because I couldn’t imagine going without my phone for a few days at this point – don’t judge me. 

Spotlight search still not working? 

If your iPhone is finished indexing – the banner in Settings will go away – and you’re still running into issues, you should review your Search settings and make sure Spotlight has access to your apps. Here’s how to check. 

Tap Settings.

Tap Search.

From here, you can adjust what shows up in Spotlight, and near the bottom of the menu, you can review which apps Spotlight has access to. You can tap into each app to grant or revoke Spotlight permission. 

However, there doesn’t seem to be a way to grant or revoke Spotlight access across all apps at once, so you have to go into each individual app to do this. 

For more on Apple, here’s what to know about iOS 27, the iPhone Duo and everything Apple announced at its “Surprise and shine” event.

title: Google goes in-depth, and a bit NSFW, on Noto 3D emoji as Android rollout expands
snippet: Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices. more…
fullText:
Google Design published a more detailed explanation of Noto 3D today as it expands beyond Pixel devices.

Google explains that the design process for Noto 3D involved “drawing, sculpting, and debating every single character by hand so that dimension never came at the cost of soul.”

Noto 3D prioritizes “emotional clarity” over “treating emoji as miniature scans of the natural world.”

Our job was to preserve the vibe behind each symbol: using 3D to give the character a body, but illustration to give it a soul.

Research found that “highly anatomical details like irises or nostril depth actually slow down how fast our brains process emotion,” so the aim was to remove “extraneous detail and [keep] facial geometry minimal.” Additionally, “excessive props and texture destroy comprehension,” with “background features and accessories” becoming “visual static” at 18×18 pixels.

	

The design team ultimately decided that “every emoji gets at most three essential details to communicate what it is.”

In going from flat assets to three dimensions, Google asked: “What does the back of a smiley face look like?” NSFW (truly) joke aside, the team found examples like how the poodle emoji only had three legs.

Meanwhile, the same research found that “people empathize far more with complete silhouettes — especially when it comes to depicting real animals.” As such, Google moved away from floating heads. 

Seeing an animal’s stance, paws, and posture helps communicate intent. Upon learning this last year, we updated a few animal emoji, like the raccoon, to embrace its full mischievous self — and now in 3D.

Following the Pixel 11 launch, Noto 3D is now “rolling out across Google apps, Android, and select devices from partners including Nothing, Lenovo, Xiaomi, OPPO, OnePlus, realme, vivo, iQOO, HONOR, TECNO, Infinix, itel, [and] Motorola.” You can also browse the entire collection on Google’s dedicated page.

title: Galaxy S26 series reportedly getting a price hike imminently, could be as much as $100
snippet: In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way. more…
fullText:
In the era of RAMageddon, the price hikes just keep coming. Samsung has left its Galaxy S26 untouched thus far, but a new report suggest prices hikes of around $100 could be on the way.

The Galaxy S26 series launched in February with the base S26 and S26+ seeing slight price bumps from their predecessors, and the Ultra unchanged – $899, $1,099, and $1,299, respectively. But a lot has changed in the time since, and it seems Samsung may be bumping those prices further up.

Hans Economy reports that, at least in Korea, Galaxy S26 prices “will be abruptly raised starting October 1.” The planned price hikes (and their converted pricing in USD) follow:

Galaxy S26: 1,254,000 won > 1,403,600 won ($930~ > $1,040)

Galaxy S26+: 1,452,000 won > 1,601,600 won ($1,077~ > $1,188~)

Galaxy S26 Ultra: 1,797,400 won > 1,947,000 won ($1,334~ > $1,444~)

Apparently, Samsung is making this move based on two factors; the continual rise of component costs, and the fact that Apple also just hiked its iPhone prices. The latest iPhone 18 Pro launches are more expensive while the iPhone 17 also saw a $100 price hike in the US (more on 9to5Mac), with the lineup now starting at $899 in the US and 1,450,000 won in South Korea.

	

With that comparison in mind, it’s harder to imagine Samsung plans to bring these price hikes to the US, as they’d make Galaxy flagships $100 more expensive than iPhones across the board, but anything’s possible. 

Samsung, commenting on the report, says that “nothing has been finalized” yet (translated):

We have not sent out any official notice regarding a price increase for the Galaxy S26 series… While it is true that we are internally reviewing whether to adjust prices in consideration of cost burdens, such as the recent rise in component prices, nothing has been finalized as of now.

title: Google Maps rolling out Android Auto speed limits and speedometer that show even without navigation
snippet: While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected. more…
fullText:
While the speedometer has been hit or miss for some Android Auto users as of late, Google Maps is now confirmed to be rolling out speed limits and a speedometer that show at all times, even when you don’t have a destination selected.

Speed limits in Google Maps launched back in 2019, with the live speedometer appearing later and only starting to show up on Android Auto a few months ago. Earlier this month, though, the speedometer vanished for some users. 

Google is now confirming two things.

First, the disappearing speedometer is being investigated by the Android Auto team. In other words, it appears to be a bug of some kind rather than an intentional removal or rollback of the feature.

	
	

More interesting, though, is that Google is rolling out the ability to see the speed limit of the current road as well as the live speedometer on Maps via Android Auto even when a destination is not set. There have been intermittent reports of this for a few weeks now, but Google is confirming that it’s actually rolling out.

…the ability to have the speedometer, speed limit, and traffic signals/stop signs showing without a destination set is still rolling out. Thus, not everyone will have this particular feature yet.

The exact timeline for when this will be widely available remains to be seen, but it’s great to see nonetheless. Drivers are very often using Google Maps navigation, but shorter or more familiar trips don’t always require setting a destination – but it’s still nice to see speed limits and the speedometer at those times.

title: Android Auto update lets you customize your Google Maps ‘driving avatar’ via car display
snippet: Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display. more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out an update for Maps on Android Auto that gives users the ability to edit their “driving avatar” directly from the car’s display.

The ability to change the classic blue arrow navigation icon in Google Maps itself is not new, but it’s only been available on car displays for about a year. In May 2025, Google Maps rolled out support for showing your chosen icon on Android Auto and CarPlay, but it needed to be set on the phone itself. 

Now, Google is rolling out an on-car picker for your Google Maps “driving avatar” on Android Auto.

The change is rather simple. Through Google Maps on Android Auto, a new “driving avatar” setting appears alongside settings for home/work and alerts. Tapping it gives you the option to pick your avatar and change it to the color of your choice. It’s the same functionality found on your phone, just now accessible directly via the car’s display.

	

This appears to be going live with a server-side update. Android Authority spotted the change with Android Auto 17.8.163744 and Google Maps 26.38.01.980791571 but, despite using those same versions, we’re not seeing the option just yet. Sound off in the comments below if you have it.

In our teardown of Android Auto 17.8, we also noticed that Google has removed the neat little “Jimothy” Easter egg which, as we predicted, was clearly never meant for a public-facing rollout.

title: I’ve Used iOS 27 for Months. Here Are 7 Things I Like and 3 I’m Still Confused About
snippet: The new OS consistently nudges things in a good direction, even if it doesn’t feel like a total overhaul.
fullText:
The latest iOS update is out now. Apple released iOS 27 on Monday, Sept. 14 (just as I predicted). The updated Siri AI is the centerpiece of the update, but the OS also brings several other features to your iPhone — even if those features aren’t especially groundbreaking.

You can download iOS 27 now by going to Settings > General > Software Update > Update Now and following the prompts on your screen.

I’ve been using iOS 27 betas since June, and found a handful of useful new features, including a new Liquid Glass slider, and even started testing the revamped Siri after avoiding the digital assistant for a decade. Overall, my phone feels snappier and opening apps is almost instantaneous. 

Apple’s iOS 27 brings a lot of quality of life upgrades to your device without as many standout new features as previous iOS updates — similar to Liquid Glass in iOS 26. There are also a few questionable changes, such as a new way to access your Notification Center, which isn’t unusual for these annual upgrades. Overall, iOS 27 is an inoffensive update filled with subtle improvements that you might not notice unless they’re pointed out.

As the official pointer-outer person, that’s my cue to give you a virtual tour around Siri AI and some of my favorite changes, as well as a few updates that left me scratching my head.

Note that my experience with these features is based on beta versions of iOS 27, so it’s possible some of them work differently on the public release. Siri AI is still in beta, even after the public release of iOS 27, and remains an opt-in experience.

iOS 27’s best improvements

Siri gets an AI overhaul

The latest iOS update has convinced me to turn over some daily digital chores to Siri, such as looking up driving directions or checking my schedule. Despite a few flaws, Siri worked well when I asked it to plot my route in CarPlay, find a cake recipe and perform a number of other simple tasks. The result? I’m now comfortable using Siri for small jobs.

In iOS 27, Siri AI is disabled by default, so you have to enable it if you want to use it. Here’s how to do so. 

Tap Settings.

Tap Siri. 

Tap Try New Siri.

It can also take time to go from being waitlisted to being able to ask Siri AI for a gift recommendation for your friend based on a text thread. Don’t forget: Siri AI is also still in beta in iOS 27, so you could run into bugs or have odd experiences with the digital assistant. Plus, Siri AI is only available in Apple Intelligence-compatible devices. iPhone 14 models or older (or the iPhone 15 or 15 Plus models) can’t access the enhanced assistant.

New Liquid Glass slider, and one questionable option

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

After Apple launched Liquid Glass in iOS 26, the company added ways to adjust transparency to address readability issues. With iOS 27, you can get as close to disabling the design as possible thanks to a new Liquid Glass slider. After installing iOS 27, you’re given an option to adjust just how liquidy or glassy you want things. But if you skip that screen, here’s where to find the Liquid Glass slider.

Tap Settings.

Tap Appearance. 

Tap Liquid Glass. 

From here, you can make Liquid Glass elements on your device more or less transparent by dragging the slider to the right. If you want more see-throughness, so elements are more transparent, drag it left. I find it difficult to tell menus and background items apart — I don’t understand who would want this option, but it’s there if you do. 

I’ve been happily using the totally frosted look (slider all the way to the right) for a few weeks now. While I didn’t mind Liquid Glass as much as other folks, the frosted setting ensures I can read and see the text, menus and icons properly. 

Safari gets an upgrade, too

My CNET colleague Jason Chun has been enjoying the Safari upgrades in iOS 27, including favorable UI tweaks. He noted that the All Tabs icon replaces the three-dot menu in Safari’s Compact toolbar. He also likes the return of the Bookmarks icon to the top of a new tab next to Reading List and History, and that Safari can automatically organize tabs. 

“It’s a super useful feature,” Chun wrote. “Especially if you keep as many emotional support tabs open as I do (currently 72).” 

More volume control across your device

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Apple finally gives you the choice to adjust the volumes of your ringtones, alerts and alarms independently. This has been greatly helpful, ensuring my alarm isn’t so loud that it wakes up my infant son at night, yet keeping my ringtone loud enough during the day that I can hear it over him crying. 

To separate the volume levels, you have to disable two switches:

Tap Settings.

Tap Sounds & Haptics.

Disable the switches next to both instances of Match Ringtone Volume.

You can then use the sliders beneath those switches to change the volume of your alarms and your alerts without affecting your ringtone volume. 

Pasting photos and links into messages is easier

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

There’s also an easy way to paste photos, links from social media and more into Messages in iOS 27. If you copy one of those things and go into a chat, Messages will display an option above your keyboard to paste the item into your message before you start typing. 

It’s a simple adjustment that streamlines texting assets to folks. Before, you had to long-press on the text box and tap Paste. That’s not a lot of steps, but tapping the option above the keyboard is faster.

I also appreciate how this makes it easier to ensure I’m pasting the intended photo or link into a message instead of another link or text from hours ago. I’ve pasted unrelated gibberish into texting fields many times before iOS 27.

The Weather app shows different elements

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

The Weather app gets another small tweak, showing more weather elements throughout the day. You can see hour-by-hour forecasts for rain and winds in your area by tapping water drop and wind symbols in the Conditions bar in the app. You can also see those conditions for the coming days of the week.

This is a welcome feature that helps me plan my day before stepping out the door with just a glance. 

New on-screen timer

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

You also don’t need to go into your clock app to set a timer in iOS 27. If you open the timer in your Control Center, a new timer window will appear at the top of your screen with a horizontal dial you can pull left or right to get the exact countdown you need (down to 15-second increments). You can set and start a timer from here and access it while in other apps. 

I like being able to quickly set and keep track of a timer without switching apps — a small but mighty improvement.

Three changes I’m still lost on

A standalone Siri app is now a thing

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

Apple Intelligence-compatible devices get a new Siri app in iOS 27 that lets you interact with the digital assistant in a similar way to other chatbots, such as Gemini on Android, and access past conversations or requests within the app.

I struggle to see the appeal of this app over the regular Siri voice assistant. It feels easier to use Siri without the app in most instances, such as asking the assistant to look up the hours of a local bookstore.

Even if you’re using the Siri app as a search engine, it feels easier to, you know… use a search engine. I asked Siri to check the news, for example, and the app would regularly give me news that was at least a few days old. This is better than when I tested an earlier beta version of iOS 27 and the app gave me news from about a month prior, but it’s still not what I’m looking for.

It does give you links at the bottom of queries to verify information, which is good if you use the app as such. However, a search engine such as DuckDuckGo could give me those links without forcing me to wade through a preamble that might be full of outdated or incorrect information.

Notification Center has a new home thanks to Siri AI

If you do enable the new Siri AI, your iPhone’s Notification Center gets a new home — much to my dismay. Instead of two sections for the drag-from-the-top touch shortcuts, now there are three. Instead of dragging down from the center of your home screen to see your notifications, now you have to drag down from the top-left corner of your home screen. If you drag down from the center, you open a new Search or Ask bar. 

I’m right-handed and this is dreadful. It’s one of the more annoying things about iOS 27. It messes with my muscle memory and my expectations of where things are located on my phone.

The good news is that if you don’t enable Siri AI (or later disable it), you can still access your Notification Center by dragging down from the top center of your home screen. It does mean you’d need to sacrifice using Siri AI — it all comes down to your UX preference. 

The tiny clock is tiny and morally wrong

Screenshot by Zach McAuliffe/CNET

You can shrink your lock screen clock in iOS 27 when customizing your lock screen. Tap the highlighted button in the picture above and the clock shrinks down into the date bar across the top of your screen. 

Sure, that option lets you see more of your lock screen background. However, I’m an advocate of the lock screen’s big clock and therefore consider the tiny clock to be heresy. Tiny clock feels too small to be comfortably legible. People who like this setting: Can you see Pluto on a clear night without a telescope?

iOS 27 is a step in the right direction

Siri AI is the centerpiece of the update, and Apple has improved on the digital assistant enough that if you don’t already use it, I’d suggest giving it another chance. Most of the other new features are small improvements and upgrades that make for a pleasant, if sometimes underwhelming, experience.

For more on the operating system, you can check out how to change some of the most annoying features on the OS and how I learned to stop worrying and began to enjoy Siri. You can also check out what could land on your device with iOS 27.2.

	

			

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Zachary McAuliffe
						

						

							Senior writer						
					

											

								

											Zach began writing for CNET in November, 2021 after writing for a broadcast news station in his hometown, Cincinnati, for five years. You can usually find him hanging out with his wife, son and dog. You can reach him at zmcauliffe@cnet.com.

title: iPhone 18 Pro Launch Could Be the First of Many for Apple’s New CEO This Year
snippet: The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max may be the first phones to go on sale under new Apple CEO John Ternus, but today’s launch hinted at even more hardware launches to come.
fullText:
New Apple CEO John Ternus welcomed buyers of the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max to the company’s flagship Fifth Avenue store in New York on Friday, and it’s likely to be just the first of several major product launches for the former hardware lead’s first year in the top job.

Dressed in a dark gray shirt and blue jeans, Ternus immediately took to taking selfies, giving handshakes and signing phone boxes for the hundreds of fans who chose to preorder the new iPhone or Apple Watch. 

	

			

Ternus, formerly Apple’s senior vice president of hardware engineering, took a casual and personable approach to the launch — even gently laughing as one excited Apple fan accidentally dropped his iPhone 17 Pro Max onto the concrete while walking into the store.

“It’s fine, it’s got a little ding, no crack, thank you, Ceramic Shield,” Dallen Frutchey, 18, from Virginia, said about the accidental drop just ahead of moving his data to his new iPhone 18 Pro Max. This is his fourth time attending one of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store openings, where he had met prior CEO Tim Cook a number of times. At today’s event, he got a selfie with Ternus just before the phone drop.

“I’m excited to have someone who is down in the details with the products working on things now,” Frutchey said, wearing a blue sweater that matched his new glacier blue phone.

Dallen Frutchey, 18, with his new iPhone 18 Pro Max in glacier blue.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

The very first person to come out of the Apple store — Harry Sun, 21, from New Jersey — walked out with a burgundy phone while wearing a Believe pin from the Apple TV show Ted Lasso. Eric Morgan, the second person in line, came all the way from Guatemala. He was buying several phones for his family, who also made the trip but were staying at their hotel, away from the iPhone launch-day madness.

Harry Sun, 21, was the first person to walk out of Apple’s Fifth Avenue store with a new iPhone in hand.Bridget Carey/CNET

The glacier blue hue appeared to be an early crowd favorite at this store, and Apple’s flagship location had a number of visible changes to mark the occasion. The outside of the store had a color blend of burgundy along with that shade of blue — giving no love to the more traditional silver and black color variants that are also available for the 18 Pro and Pro Max.

Apple decorated the entrance to its Fifth Avenue store for the launch.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Inside, the Apple store took on more of a party vibe as it filled with the crowds that had been waiting outside. A DJ booth spinning Lady Gaga songs blasted in front of a large blue carpet area that served as a showroom for the new phones, as well as the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4.

The blue carpet showroom area for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro phones, Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and the AirPods 5.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

At the opposite end of the store, without many passersby, a small photography exhibit featuring photos taken on the iPhone 18 Pro was on display in an area that formerly served as the Apple HomePod demo area. We will see over the next few months whether new products will take over that real estate, since today’s event also marks a shift in how Apple conducts its iPhone launches.

Apple has a photography exhibition spotlighting images taken on the iPhone 18 Pro at its Fifth Avenue store.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

Apple’s set to do at least one more store launch like this when the iPhone Duo goes on sale on Oct. 23 — marking the company’s first entry into the foldable phone space. It’s also rumored to be launching a number of new home entertainment products, with the decreased floor space for the HomePod possibly hinting at a relaunch of the speaker now that the new Siri AI assistant is rolling out to the iPhone 15 Pro and later.

And that’s not to mention the rumors hinting that a non-Pro iPhone 18 and an iPhone Air sequel may be set up for a spring launch, anchoring what could be a new annual launch event early in the year to contrast with premium phones coming later in Apple’s typical September window.

Apple’s current lineup consists of (left to right) the iPhone 17, iPhone Air, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Not pictured but also available are the iPhone 17E and iPhone 16.Mike Sorrentino/CNET

So while this is the first iPhone launch under Ternus, it’s likely that several more of these are to come over the next year.

Bridget Carey contributed to this story.

New Apple CEO John Ternus welcomed buyers of the new iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max to the company’s flagship Fifth Avenue store in New York on Friday, and it’s likely to be just the first of several major product launches for the former hardware lead’s first year in the top job.

Dressed in a dark gray shirt and blue jeans, Ternus immediately took to taking selfies, giving handshakes and signing phone boxes for the hundreds of fans who chose to preorder the new iPhone or Apple Watch.

fullText:
Andrew Liszewski

 

is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

FunnyPlaying, a Chinese company known for its Game Boy and GBA upgrade kits, has announced a new handheld that plays original Nintendo cartridges and ROMs. The FPGB Mini’s cartridge support is limited to the Game Boy and Game Boy Color so it isn’t as capable as the Analogue Pocket that’s also compatible with the GBA and Sega Game Gear. What still makes the FPGB Mini a tempting alternative is its extremely pocketable design resulting in a handheld only slightly wider than a Game Boy cartridge, and its cheaper price.

Following recent price hikes the Analogue Pocket is now $239.99 while the FPGB Mini is currently discounted from $89.99 to $69.99 for the first batch of just 20 units that quickly sold out. However, the company is potentially planning to release more following some hardware improvements, according to Retro Dodo who’s been testing the handheld for a few days and so far seems impressed with its design and capabilities.

Like the Pocket the FPGB Mini uses field-programmable gate array (FPGA) technology to play Game Boy and GBC games as accurately as Nintendo’s original hardware does. But the FPGB Mini brings improvements like a 2.98-inch, 800x720-pixel LCD display, an 1,800mAh rechargeable battery, and a microSD slot for storing game saves, screenshots, or ROMs that can be played through emulation. The handheld’s compact size does prevent cartridges with rumble motors or other hardware additions from being used, but otherwise the FPGB Mini looks to be about as small as the Game Boy is ever going to get.

title: Apple explains how the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode works
snippet: A new post on Apple’s Security Research blog details the fascinating tech, architecture, and thinking behind the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode. Here are the details more…
fullText:
A new post on Apple’s Security Research blog details the fascinating tech, architecture, and thinking behind the iPhone 18 Pro’s new Reference Image camera mode. Here are the details

Apple explains why it developed the new Reference Image camera mode

In a blog post titled “Apple Reference Image: A New Approach for Verified Photography,” Apple goes in-depth into how its new photographic authenticity system works.

The post confirms that the company’s motivation to build Apple Reference Image was the ever-lowering barrier to creating or adjusting images synthetically.

Apple explains that while industry standards such as C2PA help address the problem, they remain vulnerable to compromise at points in the editing chain.

For this reason, Apple developed a fascinatingly creative chain-of-verification system that is private, secure, and, to the company’s knowledge, “the only image provenance system that provides quantum-secure defenses.”

‘A new standard for verifiable digital photography’

In its explanation, Apple uses classic photography terms, such as a secure digital negative, which contains the raw captured pixels along with information such as signed metadata and timestamps, and is developed in a secure, private, and verifiable environment within the company’s Private Cloud Compute structure.

This semantic authenticity is just one of the three core requirements Apple says a high-assurance photographic provenance system must meet, the other two being resilience to compromise and privacy preservation.

If Apple’s confidence scoring system identifies a sensor as low-scoring and that sensor is revoked, Private Cloud Compute will no longer sign Reference Images captured by it.

Likewise, individual Reference Images can be revoked if later determined to be fraudulent, with Apple devices regularly fetching updated revocation lists.

Another interesting aspect of the Apple Reference Image chain of trust is that it begins once a camera sensor is first initialized, during the iPhone’s manufacturing process.

The sensor generates a signing key pair, keeping the private key to itself while sharing the public verification key with the factory recording station, which then signs it with a factory certificate authority and records it in the device’s hardware manifest.

That private key will later be used to sign every photo taken in Reference Image mode, binding the captured pixel data and sensor metadata to that specific camera sensor before the image ever reaches iOS for further processing.

Apple also uses cryptographic timestamps to establish a verifiable window for when each photo was taken. Instead of relying on a timestamp provided by the device’s general operating system, which the company says can be compromised, the iPhone periodically receives a secure timestamp token that serves as a lower bound.

It then requests another after capture to establish an upper bound, allowing Apple to verify that the image was captured sometime between the two.

The Secure Enclave also plays a role by signing metadata that originates outside the camera sensor. Private Cloud Compute later verifies those signatures, confirms that the sensor and Secure Enclave belong to the same iPhone, and checks the timestamps before developing the secure digital negative.

Once those checks pass, Private Cloud Compute processes the negative into the final JPEG Reference Image and signs it using a combination of traditional and post-quantum cryptography, which Apple says is designed to keep the image verifiable even against future quantum attacks.

Apple goes on to explain that the Reference Image framework was designed so that an outside observer cannot determine the identity of the photographer, which device took a given photo, or whether the same device captured two Reference Images.

This is particularly important, Apple notes, for photographers working in sensitive environments, such as conflict zones, where proving an image is authentic should not require giving up anonymity.

This Security Research blog post makes for a truly fascinating read, even if you are not a technical person. You can read it here.

title: iOS 27’s Wallet app adds feature that will make you want to use Apple Cash
snippet: Apple Wallet is better than ever in iOS 27 thanks to a handful of new features, including a clever solution for splitting bills with friends and family via Apple Cash. Here’s how it works. more…
fullText:
Apple Wallet is better than ever in iOS 27 thanks to a handful of new features, including a clever solution for splitting bills with friends and family via Apple Cash. Here’s how it works.

iOS 27 uses your iPhone’s camera and Apple Intelligence to make bill splitting seamless

Apple Cash has been part of iOS for years now, and I use it occasionally with a select few people in my life. But third-party services like Venmo and Zelle still tend to be preferred by most people I know for sending money.

In iOS 27 though, a new Apple Wallet bill splitting feature could make Apple Cash far more popular.

Here’s how the new bill splitting option works, per Apple:

With iOS 27, users can split bills using Apple Cash and Apple Intelligence, making it easy to settle up after meals with friends. Users can simply scan a receipt with their iPhone camera, or use a photo of a bill to split it with friends. This capability is available in Messages, in Apple Wallet, or by using Visual Intelligence onscreen and with the iPhone camera. For example, the new Siri mode in the Camera app lets users get information and take action on what’s in front of them. When users point their iPhone at a receipt using Siri mode, it can surface the relevant action to split a bill with Apple Cash and identify the items on the receipt. As users select their items, their total payment is calculated, including their share of tax and tip, so they can pay back exactly what they owe with Apple Cash.

The whole process is extremely simple and seamless. Just point your iPhone camera at a receipt, or choose an existing receipt photo, and Apple Intelligence does the work of identifying each item so you can mark what’s yours. It’s easy to add a tip too, with no math required as iOS 27 calculates common amounts like 18% and 20% automatically.

In my testing, bill splitting has proven an excellent addition to iOS 27 that delivers a very user-friendly experience. I love that it works from the standard Camera app in Siri mode, via the Messages app, and of course in Wallet directly.

The only real downside is that if you or your friends haven’t set up Apple Cash yet, that will be an extra step that slows you down. 

But once Apple Cash is set up, bill splitting is a great addition that I hope gains a lot of popularity over time because the experience is so seamless.

Have you tried bill splitting in iOS 27? How did it go? Let us know in the comments.

title: Samsung Gallery rolling out Google Photos sync, here are the details you need to know
snippet: As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting. more…
fullText:
As teased, Samsung Gallery is now rolling out support for Google Photos sync, though there are a few details worth noting.

Through app updates earlier this week, Samsung confirmed it was replacing the Microsoft OneDrive backup integration in its Gallery app with Google Photos sync. The change wasn’t live at the time, but works similarly to integrations found in the pre-installed Gallery apps on other phones from other Android brands such as OnePlus and Xiaomi.

Now, it’s actually starting to roll out.

Following updates to the Gallery Sync and Samsung Cloud apps, a Samsung Gallery update is also now rolling out to some users, which enables Google Photos integration – we’re not yet seeing the update on our end. Ice Universe shared screenshots of the settings.

	

Samsung Gallery v15.9.01.7 seems to be the trigger for activating sync, despite other apps actually facilitating the sync.

On a support page, Google offers more details on how Samsung Gallery > Google Photos sync works. It requires your Samsung device to be running Android 13 or newer, doesn’t support Workspace accounts, and there are some restrictions on what media you can see and what features work.

Google says that images and videos synced from Samsung Gallery won’t work with Memories and highlights, Live albums, or Search in Google Photos. Samsung Gallery also won’t show content backed up directly through Photos – only content synced from Samsung Gallery via a Samsung device shows up in the app.

Samsung has access to the media items that were originally backed up from Gallery Cloud Sync, but not to other items in Google Photos that were not backed up from a synced Samsung device.

If your device has all of the needed updates, you’ll find the option to enable Google Photos sync in Samsung Gallery via Menu > Settings > Sync > Sync photos and videos.

Samsung Gallery’s integration with OneDrive ends on September 30 for those still using it.

title: Android Bench 2.0 focuses on long-horizon tasks, agent evaluations
snippet: Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks. more…
fullText:
Google’s development of Android Bench continues today with a version 2.0 that reflects how AI can handle more complex development tasks.

The first version “focused on incremental changes to existing repositories,” like bug fixes or smaller feature requests. Android Bench 2.0 targets “tasks of great complexity that take an engineer multiple days or even a week to complete,” such as adding new features, building apps from scratch, and converting cross-platform apps to Android.

This new focus required “more nuanced evaluation and scoring” that goes beyond pass or fail grading. Google is moving from binary to continuous scoring:

We calculate this completion rate through a combination of factors like functionality, visual fidelity, and avoiding regressions. We also apply objective scoring penalties for deviations from evaluation instructions or structural constraints.

Google has rated Gemini 3.7/3.8 Flash, OpenAI GPT-6, Anthropic Fable 5.1, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8 Max. GPT-6 Astra is at the top of the benchmark with a 28% pass rate (compared to scores in the 90% range with the previous approach).

	

Google shared insights like how “porting cross-platform apps to Android remains an open challenge—no model hits a 100% pass rate, and frontier models reach at most a 80% completion rate.”

“…AI does a better job at writing new code rather than refactoring existing code. Refactors and migrations get trickier because success depends on architectural complexity rather than code volume.”

“Models show strong capabilities on well-established, deterministic transformations, such as converting Java to Kotlin, swapping Retrofit for Ktor, or introducing a ViewModel layer.”

“…models struggle when tasks require runtime validation (like missing dependency injection graphs), involve breaking framework changes, or run into knowledge gaps with unreleased libraries.”

With agent evaluations, Android Bench ran “agents from the corresponding model provider,” like Gemini 3.8 Flash on Google Antigravity and GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex. Google says “harness design positively impacts developer outcomes,” with Android Bench planning to include different model and agent combinations in the future.

title: Valve’s open-source ‘Lepton’ brings Android games to the $1,059 Steam Frame
snippet: Valve has just released its Lepton tool as an open-source resource for bringing Android-native games to Linux and, in turn, Steam. more…
fullText:
Valve has just released its Lepton tool as an open-source resource for bringing Android-native games to Linux and, in turn, Steam.

On GitHub, Valve has released Lepton as an open-source repository, allowing developers to use the tool primarily for porting games to the Steam Frame. Valve explains:

Lepton is a tool for use with the Steam client which allows games which are exclusive to Android to run on the Linux operating system. Most users should use Lepton provided by the Steam Client itself.

…Lepton is intended to help game developers bring their VR Android games to the Steam Frame. Other usecases are possible, but were not the focus of development and may lack polish.

The Verge points out that some developers are already using Lepton to port Meta Quest games (the Quest runs Android) to the Steam Frame.

The Steam Frame officially made its debut earlier this week, with the Snapdragon-powered VR headset coming in at a cost of $1,059. A waitlist is now open.

title: Tim Cook keeping John Ternus away from controversy by attending White House dinner
snippet: One of the trickier parts of Tim Cook’s job when he was Apple CEO was walking the tightrope of upholding the company’s values without provoking the ire of the White House over things like immigration policy and DEI. His new role as executive chairman sees him retain responsibility for government liaison, offering replacement CEO John Ternus some degree of protection … more…
fullText:
One of the trickier parts of Tim Cook’s job when he was Apple CEO was walking the tightrope of upholding the company’s values without provoking the ire of the White House over things like immigration policy and DEI.

His new role as executive chairman sees him retain responsibility for government liaison, offering replacement CEO John Ternus some degree of protection … 

Past challenges

The challenges Cook faced in the past date back many years. For example, back in 2018, changes to US immigration policy and practice affected thousands of Apple employees. Tim Cook was among a number of CEOs who wrote to the administration stating that the changes were causing “considerable anxiety for many thousands of Apple employees,” as well as “threatening to disrupt company operations.”

Cook faced similar difficulties last year when Trump said that Apple should get rid of its DEI policies. He responded by saying the company would comply with any changes to the law but would not compromise its values.

Cook is now Apple’s official diplomat

Earlier this year, Apple confirmed that Cook’s new role includes responsibility for liaising with governments.

As executive chairman, Cook will assist with certain aspects of the company, including engaging with policymakers around the world.

Attending White House dinner next week

Bloomberg reports that Cook will be attending a White House state dinner for China’s president next week. The event takes place at a difficult time for US-China relations, especially over AI.

Apple Inc. Executive Chairman Tim Cook and OpenAI Chief Executive Officer Sam Altman are poised to attend a White House state dinner for Chinese President Xi Jinping next week […] The summit comes at a delicate moment for US-Chinese relations — and the artificial intelligence industry. Geopolitical tensions are simmering over the AI race, international trade and the Middle East.

9to5Mac’s Take

I would wager a large sum of money that the idea of the diplomatic role being Cook’s responsibility came from the man himself. It’s a self-sacrificing move intended to free his successor from unnecessary distractions and controversies.

Ternus will of course still be constrained in what he can say when it comes to Apple’s response to controversial policies and laws, whether in the US, China or elsewhere, but having official responses be the responsibility of someone else does give him more latitude than would otherwise be the case.

snippet: Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview. more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m finding some peace playing Lumines Remastered, deciding whether to get my kids one of the new 4th-gen Yoto players, and trying to figure out why everyone is freaking out about this recent Tom Cruise interview.

As a reminder, Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Over the past few months, I’ve been using MCP (Model Context Protocol) to connect with my bank, my to-do app (TickTick), my personal database (Obsidian), and anything else I can get my hands on. I find it intuitive to have a conversation with a chatbot about stacking tasks, performing a complex set of calculations, or just figuring out the answer to a difficult problem. 

	

Now Google is getting in on the MCP action with Home MCP, a way to connect coding agents like Claude, Codex, Antigravity, Hermes, and OpenClaw to Google’s Home ecosystem and the products connected to it.

Right now, the tool is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced subscribers in the US, but it’s an ambitious first step toward making it easier to interact with what is usually a digital rat’s nest of brands, categories, and compatibility layers. Google has already rolled out Gemini for Home in an attempt to make automation more straightforward, but I commend the company for dipping its toe into the DIY space and seeing what happens.

According to Google, MCP “gives your favorite AI agent real-world physical context—allowing it to analyze and answer questions about home activity, summarize camera footage across rooms, manage devices on your behalf, or even create your own smart home dashboards using everyday language.” I’m totally going to use it to teach my Nest Cam Outdoor that the cat who wanders onto my driveway every morning isn’t, in fact, a person. Wish me luck.

It’s iPhone review season, and because this seems like an “S” year, the camera is rightfully getting the most attention. That’s why I watched basically every second of all the new iPhone 18 Pro reviews from channels like PetaPixel, Tyler Stalman, The Verge, and Matti Haapoja.

I’m still not sure what to think about the aperture control. Most reviews are saying that it has very little real-world utility, while others are claiming that it was the only way to offer an f/1.48 lens without sacrificing depth control (or overly relying on software bokeh). Either way, once Apple decides to offer a hardware feature it tends to stick around whether or not it’s any good (see Camera Control), so we’ll likely see a few more generations of this tech.

Sticking with the iPhone theme, two of my favorite podcasters convened this week to discuss the iPhone Duo and how it fares next to the multitude of Android competitors. 

(And if you enjoy the conversation with Stephen Radochia and want to hear more from him, he and I host a little podcast called Old’s Cool that looks at new tech from a vintage point of view.)

➡️ FWD:

This section has some of our favorite stuff from around the internet. Great videos, weird memes, fun reads, recommended apps, whatever. Send us your recommendations!

Tired of getting recorded against your will by other meeting attendees? Kalypta from Deveillance reportedly makes you “inaudible to AI” by “reshaping audio in real time” on your local machine. What a crazy world we live in.

OpenAI’s “Project Lily” tasks real humans with reading ChatGPT transcripts in order to make inference better and more accurate. According to 404 Media, which broke the story, “OpenAI is hiring hundreds of contractors who read a massive stream of real users’ ChatGPT prompts, with the prompts sometimes including sensitive personal information.” 

Snap finally let people try its $2,200 Specs smart glasses, a bulky and unwieldy computer that it’s inviting developers to test. The gadget has a 4-hour battery and can run real apps like Spotify while relying on a proactive AI assistant to do everything else.

Over the past couple of days, I’ve been trying out a new launcher on my Fold 8, a launcher unlike anything I’ve used on Android before. That’s because it’s defined by its adherence to the UX found on iOS — specifically the upcoming iPhone Duo.

From the demented mind of Reddit’s u/wolftech029, Folio is a love letter (for better or worse) to the way Apple’s home screen drastically differs from the ones found on various Android phones. From predefined grids to Apple’s App Library to the Duo’s funky blur effect, Folio has it all. 

I’m not sure it’s going to stay on my phone for long, but its existence (and the speed at which it was vibe-coded) is a testament to Android’s versatility and openness.

title: iOS 27.2 references new option to overwrite iPhone storage with blank data after erasing
snippet: Apple is working on a new option to more thoroughly wipe an iPhone’s storage when erasing the device, but there’s a catch. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple is working on a new option to more thoroughly wipe an iPhone’s storage when erasing the device, but there’s a catch. Here are the details.

New feature exclusive to Chinese devices

References included in today’s iOS 27.2 beta 1 point to a new iPhone erasing option that will let the user overwrite the device’s entire storage with blank data, including storage that isn’t actively in use.

In addition to erasing the iPhone’s data, the feature can overwrite the device’s entire storage with blank data, including storage that isn’t actively in use. Apple warns that the process may take longer than a standard erase and could affect the device’s lifespan.

The move is interesting, as currently, when a user erases an iPhone, the device’s encryption keys are destroyed, effectively rendering the remaining data inaccessible. In fact, Apple is very clear about this in an Apple Platform Deployment support article:

On the device, erasing (or wiping) obliterates all the keys in effaceable storage and renders all user data cryptographically inaccessible.

While digging through today’s beta, 9to5Mac confirmed that, as currently implemented, the feature will only be available on iPhone models sold in China, where Apple appears to be adding it to comply with an upcoming data-erasure requirement.

That’s because a new Chinese standard taking effect on January 1, 2027, will require smartphones and other electronic devices to offer a way to more thoroughly erase stored data, including through methods such as overwriting it.

For semiconductor storage, such as the flash storage used in smartphones, one approved method involves overwriting storage containing user data at least once with meaningless data. That closely matches Apple’s description of replacing storage with blank data.

Finally, the new erasing option won’t be exclusive to iPhones, as code references also point to support for other devices, including the iPad, HomePod, and Apple Vision Pro.

To learn more about China’s upcoming GB 46864-2025 standard, follow this link.

title: iOS 27 adds three new iPhone features you’ll use all the time
snippet: iOS 27 launched this week as a major iPhone update, here are three new features that could be among the most-used for many users. more…
fullText:
iOS 27 launched this week as a major iPhone update, here are three new features that could be among the most-used for many users.

#1: Siri AI

Whatever your opinion of Siri has been in the past, iOS 27’s Siri AI is different.

Siri didn’t just get an AI glow-up with a few upgrades. Apple says it “tore [Siri] to the ground” and “rebuilt it from the ground up.”

You can now ask Siri about anything, like you might ask Google or ChatGPT, and it provides informed, helpful answers. It can also perform way more actions on your iPhone than before, and works seamlessly and consistently across all your devices. There’s also a dedicated Siri app to hold all your conversations.

I’ve been using iOS 27’s new Siri for three full months, and it’s became a daily go-to for me.

#2: Automatic proofreading, including for grammar

The iPhone has long offered a basic spellcheck feature that underlines any words it identifies as misspelled. Now in iOS 27, Apple is expanding proofreading in two ways:

spellcheck is now powered by Apple Intelligence  

there’s a new tool for checking grammar

AI being applied to spellcheck means even if a word is technically spelled correctly, you’ll see suggested word replacements if your iPhone thinks the word is being used incorrectly.

Whereas misspellings are typically underlined in red, suggested word replacements and grammar issues are underlined in blue. Compared to common typos, this makes them feel more like optional suggestions rather than in-your-face warning signs.

If you’re not a fan, you can always disable proofreading in Settings. But I’d guess that for lots of users, these features will be welcome iOS 27 additions.

#3: Search overhaul in Spotlight, Photos, and Mail

Search is one of the most essential features for most apps, and certainly for the iPhone as a whole. And in iOS 27, Spotlight search has received a major overhaul.

In addition to having Siri fully integrated with Spotlight, the iPhone’s systemwide search has been rebuilt with a more comprehensive index of your content that always stays up to date throughout the day.

This means you should find Spotlight more useful than ever, as it offers better and more relevant results with every search. Apple says that the same new search foundation powering Spotlight has been implemented in the Photos and Mail apps too, upgrading search across those key apps. So far in my testing, I can very much tell the difference.

Which iOS 27 features are your early favorites so far? Let us know in the comments.

title: DoorDash Can Now Deliver Your Ginormous Costco Order the Same Day
snippet: Uber Eats also expanded its Costco delivery service from 17 states to 47.
fullText:
Ready to get your 1-gallon jug of ketchup and 12-month supply of toilet paper delivered to your door? 

Starting Thursday, DoorDash will offer same-day delivery from every Costco warehouse in the US, the online delivery service said. The announcement comes a day after Uber Eats said it was expanding its Costco delivery from 17 states to 47. DoorDash customers need to have a Costco membership, which costs $65 for the Gold Star plan and $135 for the Executive plan. 

To get started in the DoorDash app, search for Costco and select your local warehouse. Then link the Costco membership and complete the order. The process is basically the same for Uber Eats users.

DoorDash said “groceries, pantry staples, household essentials, electronics, seasonal merchandise, Kirkland Signature products and more” will be available for delivery. Delivery fees will vary, depending on the order, and DashPass members will get free delivery on eligible orders.

Costco has had a delivery partnership with Instacart since 2013. Instacart users don’t need a Costco membership, though they’ll likely pay higher prices than members.

Read more: The 9 Best Grocery Delivery Services of 2026

DoorDash was already delivering Costco products in Australia, New Zealand, Sweden, Iceland and Puerto Rico, and the company added the US to the list after seeing that “Costco” was among the most-searched retailers by app users.

Online grocery delivery trends

Online grocery delivery has been growing fast in recent years. Peapod, HomeGrocer and Webvan tried and failed in the early years of the dot-com boom, partly because of slow internet speeds and high infrastructure costs. But the COVID pandemic triggered a massive surge in the e-grocery business. 

After the nationwide lockdown started in early 2020, monthly online grocery sales in the US jumped to $6.5 billion, up from $2 billion before the pandemic. More than 57% of US households bought groceries online, compared to 25% prior to the lockdown.

Though many returned to brick-and-mortar stores, online grocery shopping has started to pick up again, thanks to deliveries that are faster and more streamlined than ever. Some items from Amazon come in 30 minutes or less, and Walmart also offers half-hour delivery in several US markets. Gopuff delivers convenience items such as snacks, drinks and cleaning products, with thousands in as fast as 15 minutes.

Online grocery sales increased more than 20% year over year for six consecutive quarters through March of this year.

Many US households are also turning more to Costco (and Walmart) as prices continue to rise for groceries, electronics, gas and pretty much everything else. Market research firm Placer.ai said trips to Costco are up by more than 18% since 2019, and Consumer Reports rated Costco and Walmart as offering the best value for groceries.

Concern for Dashers

The DoorDash-Costco partnership is a great new opportunity for delivery workers, but both companies have to make it a win-win for drivers, says Peter Schlactus, co-founder and executive director of the Association for Delivery Drivers. A4DD provides safety training, discounted gear and insurance, and job opportunities for members.

“DoorDash and Costco should together ensure that driver treatment and working conditions meet the highest standards, enabling dedicated drivers to support themselves comfortably as they deserve,” Schlactus told CNET. 

“In their haste to recruit drivers, many gig apps minimize what they ask of drivers and safety training is often a casualty. This puts both drivers and the public at risk, especially given the time pressures that this work entails.”

According to the company’s website, DoorDash drivers (called “Dashers”) receive 100% of all customer tips, including those earned on DoorDash Drive orders.

title: I Got the Inside Scoop on Apple’s New Health App, Now in Developer Beta
snippet: I spoke with Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, to learn more about the redesigned Health app and its new features.
fullText:
Last week at Apple’s “Surprise and Shine” event, Dr. Sumbul Desai, Apple’s VP of Health and Fitness, announced the redesigned Health app and its fresh features. Between the new Insights tab with Apple Intelligence-powered suggestions, a Longevity tab that shows your Health Age, a readiness score, movement assessments, a blood panel and curated doctor videos, my head was swimming with questions. The following day, I sat down for a video chat with Desai for deeper insight into Apple’s reimagined health platform.

On Wednesday, the new Health app debuted in the first developer beta of iOS 27.2. Some announced features will be available in later betas, including personalized summaries under the Insights tab, personalized recommendations and the ability to order a blood panel from Quest Diagnostics. 

“Features will roll out progressively,” Apple said in an email. “Feedback during the beta period will help us continue refining it ahead of the public release in late 2026.”

Here’s everything you can expect to uncover in the Health app and the features you shouldn’t sleep on.

From data spreadsheet to intelligent experience

Launched in 2014, the Health app was initially intended to be like a spreadsheet, with data flowing in, Desai explained. However, the team realized they wanted more from the app, so it evolved over the past 12 years into what Desai now calls “an experience.”

Those at the helm of the Health app’s 2026 makeover considered how to leverage Apple’s machine learning and AI to help people live healthier, while also personalizing the app’s recommendations and turning it into an intelligent hub, not unlike the iPhone itself. For instance, as you open the app and move through your day, different screens appear to reflect your health status. 

Movement assessments have also been added to provide an even more complete picture of a user’s health and track progress or decline. Desai described them as a “mini physical” you can complete at home.

All assessments under the app’s Longevity tab are science-based and contribute to a rainbow-petal visual that illuminates your state of health. Some assessments rely on vision-based AI models that integrate the phone’s camera, marking the first time Apple has used the camera for health.  

The current iteration of the Health app is just the beginning and was designed to set in motion the next era of the team’s work in health and fitness, as Desai said those working on the app still feel they have more to do.

The Longevity tab’s rainbow visual.Apple

Health Age: Biological vs. birthday

One standout feature from Apple’s event was the Health app’s Longevity tab, which will include a feature called Health Age that uses health metrics such as your VO2 max (the maximum amount of oxygen your body consumes during exercise), resting heart rate, sleep and heart rate variability, along with lab data such as LDL cholesterol and A1c for your average blood sugar level, to provide your biological age, which represents how your body is aging on a cellular level when compared to your actual age. 

Apple’s own Heart and Movement Study, which it applies across all its health products, informs both Health Age and Readiness, which uses your activity data, daytime and overnight vitals and sleep data to tell you about your capacity for the day ahead. 

The five-year Heart and Movement Study was conducted in collaboration with the American Heart Association and Brigham and Women’s Hospital to explore the connection between heart health and physical activity. Apple used that data to create the normative ranges for the insights it provides in the app.

While Desai acknowledged the Health Age assessment is more of a “fun way to look at your health habits” and that no one can tell you your actual biological age, it’s another way to provide insight and suggest healthy habits users can integrate into their lives. 

I’m also hoping my Health Age is lower than my actual age. Apple

Apple’s secret sauce

Apple isn’t the first company to offer features such as a readiness score or biological age, but Desai said that it stands out from competitors because of its unique perspectives, experiences and the science behind its work. 

“When we first started our work in health, when we announced our irregular heart rhythm notifications and ECG, those were clinically validated scientific features,” she said. Desai likened those early days to building a muscle that lets the team create impactful products the medical community will appreciate, and users can easily understand.

That muscle Apple first built has been exercised with all the Health app’s new features, as Desai said that everything is rooted in science. On her team, for instance, physical therapists graded each movement in the app’s mobility assessments to ensure that when a movement is picked up and a result is given, it’s graded the way an actual physical therapist would grade it. 

Uniting science and expertise, Desai said that’s what Apple brings to the table, and its Health app experience. 

The new Health app’s ‘sleeper hit’

Much of the discourse following Apple’s event has been about the new readiness score and Health Age. I was curious what Desai felt was the “sleeper hit” feature that didn’t get as much attention. 

“It’s actually the assessments,” Desai said. “You’re going to be able to, on a regular basis, do a push-up test and a core test and see if you’re improving. Then we give you insights and things that you can do to improve, and then you can test again. It’s almost like having a physical therapist or a trainer.”

The VO2 max test, in particular, marks the first time Apple’s doing an on-demand, in-the-moment VO2 max test. 

You can then take all your assessment results, and the Health app will put them into a report you can share with your doctor. 

A person performing a movement assessment using their iPhone.Apple/Screenshot by CNET

Homing in on your body’s big players

Based on its new assessments, the Longevity tab’s visualization has seven tabs: heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement health, metabolic health, hearing and nutrition. But how did Apple narrow it down to those seven?

“We picked areas where we felt like we had the appropriate data to comment on,” Desai explained. “For example, we do a cardiovascular risk score through some of the questions. It’s based on traditional risk scores and cardiovascular risk scores that are done.”

The team prioritized information they believe people will use and assessments they’ll complete, while ensuring the chosen health areas feel holistic and will help people concerned about long-term quality of life.

“There’s still more that we think we can do, but this is where we’re starting,” Desai stated. In other words, Longevity’s rainbow visual could gain more colors in the future. 

Keeping privacy at Apple’s core

When it comes to its Health app, Desai said privacy is where they start and end. 

“Candidly, we may not always be the first to market, but when we release something, we can stand behind it from a privacy standpoint,” Desai stated. “All the features you saw [announced] are no different. … It’s part of the conversation every day, and up till the day that the products are launched.”

Apple will hold off on releasing a product if it hasn’t met its privacy bar. The team behind the Health app also uses a checks-and-balances system, having other teams review their work to ensure they are nailing their privacy approach. 

“In this world where more things happen in the cloud, we want to make sure that’s all encrypted and private, which is why we have Private Cloud Compute,” said Desai. Private Cloud Compute is Apple’s cloud intelligence system designed for private AI processing.

The team’s approach is end-to-end because privacy matters for all your data, not just health data. 

Apple Intelligence has suggestions

The Health app’s new Insights tab uses Apple Intelligence to analyze your health metrics and provide a timely summary that updates throughout the day. 

“We also make suggestions,” said Desai. “For example, if you have an injury or you’re trying to work on your mobility, we’ll give you suggestions on the types of exercises you might be doing.”

It’s another example of how the app is evolving from a database to something that more closely resembles a personalized health advisor.

The daily insights are meant to be bite-size pieces of information that are one small thing you can do for your health each day. Some days these insights may be interesting; other days, you might be given information you already know.

Under Insights, the For You section will use your data to offer personalized recommendations and relevant articles.Apple

Health on a cellular level, explained

For $119, the new Health app will let you purchase a blood panel with over 50 biomarkers through Quest Diagnostics. You can also get your blood pressure, height, weight and waist and hip circumferences measured. All this helps provide a more complete picture of metabolic health.

The revamped app will include videos from doctors that help people better understand what they see in the app. 

“When you get your assessment results, you’ll actually see your own data in the videos where they’re explained by clinicians,” said Desai. “We have a physician, a physical therapist, a sleep expert, a mental health expert. The reason we did that is, for certain things, gamification works, but for certain things, you just want to know the information in an easy-to-understand way from an authoritative resource.”

While an expert explains the subject at hand, your health data, whether from your labs or your Apple Watch, will be overlaid on the video so you can see it as you learn more. 

Ultimately, Desai doesn’t see the future of the Health app as one size fits all. Depending on the feature, the team always chooses what makes health as accessible and understandable as possible. In a world with an abundance of health data, perhaps that’s what matters most: ensuring people understand the numbers they see on their devices, and knowing what to do with them once the screen goes black. 

		

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Anna Gragert
						

						

							Senior Editor, Health and Home

Over the past 12 years, Anna has also written for the LA Times, Elle, Bust Magazine, Dazed, Apartment Therapy, Well+Good and more. title: OpenAI and Microsoft knew they were starting a ‘doom loop’ for the web
snippet: Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times' case against OpenAI and Microsoft are pretty damning. The companies' own documentation warned that it was starting a "doom loop" that would damage the web, characterized its scraping of data to train its models as the "largest theft of labor in human history," and that it made a "complete mockery of the idea of fair use." Many of the most eye-catching quotes from the document come from Microsoft's Director of Applied Science, Brent Hecht. Though, the company has tried to distance itself from Hecht's assertions. Microsoft spokesperson Alex Haurek told The Verge that "These comments ref … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Recently unsealed court documents in the New York Times’ case against OpenAI and Microsoft are pretty damning. The companies’ own documentation warned that it was starting a “doom loop” that would damage the web, characterized its scraping of data to train its models as the “largest theft of labor in human history,” and that it made a “complete mockery of the idea of fair use.”

Many of the most eye-catching quotes from the document come from Microsoft’s Director of Applied Science, Brent Hecht. Though, the company has tried to distance itself from Hecht’s assertions. Microsoft spokesperson Alex Haurek told The Verge that “These comments reflect one employee’s individual perspective, are not a legal analysis, and do not represent the company’s views.”

In a separate court filing, Jordan Usdan, GM for Data Strategy and Ops at Microsoft AI, characterized Hecht’s role as adversarial. He said that Hecht “holds divergent, academic, and forward-looking views about how data ecosystems for AI should operate and is employed at Microsoft to bring asymmetrical, futuristic, and academic points of view … nor is he someone who speaks for Microsoft specifically as to his theoretical views on AI’s potential effect on content creators.”

But whether or not Microsoft wants to own these comments, it’s clear that this came true. Google Zero is real! AI is eating the web!

There are plenty more wild statements in NYT’s filing from a variety of figures, including Satya Nadella, Sam Altman, and other OpenAI employees. Here are some highlights from the 92 page document.

“An astonishing theft”

The introduction quotes Hecht and OpenAI’s Head of ChatGPT (presumably Nick Turley) in a way that seems to show the companies knew they posed an “existential threat” to publishers like the New York Times. Hecht calls ChatGPT and Copilot’s harvesting of data the “largest theft of labor in human history” and says that Microsoft’s defense makes a “complete mockery of the idea of ‘fair use.’”

It’s a “doom loop”

Satya Nadella admits that chatbots have basically replaced search and removed the need to go straight to the source for info. But perhaps more damning is an internal Microsoft document that says, “Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time: It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.’”

That’s not even a real number

Don’t be fooled by OpenAI or Microsoft’s claims of altruistic intent. OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman is more interested in the “gazillions” of dollars it he could potentially make through commercial AI.

Paywall shmaywall

Despite Nadella later being quoted as saying, “anything that is paywalled should be licensed,” An OpenAI representative admitted that he was “unaware” of any effort to detect or remove paywalled content from training data.

“Insanely good at regurgitation”

Internally, it seems that OpenAI was well aware of ChatGPT’s tendency to simply reproduce copyrighted material “verbatim.” Even though it acknowledged that the “prevention of memorization” was important to “minimize copyright violations,” employees admitted that GPT-4 “memorized a ton of data and therefore will be insanely good at regurgitation.”

The filing then goes on to cite several examples of ChatGPT outputting long strings of copy straight from articles in the Times, Mercury News, The Denver Post, LifeHacker, and Eurogamer in response to queries.

“‘Hoovering up’ all their work”

Microsoft knew how its wholesale scraping of the internet would be perceived and admitted that “almost no one intended for they [sic] content they created to be used in this fashion, nor are they compensated for its use.”

A “substitute for the labor of people”

OpenAI Policy Director Jack Clark saw the writing on the wall, saying that it was “creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” Internal documents described ChatGPT as “the modern newsstand.” OpenAI’s Nick Turley is later quoted as saying that once you get an answer from its chatbot, there is “no good reason to click” on a link to the source.

Destroying their own supply chain

Microsoft is quoted as admitting that “LLMs are a product that destroys its own supply chain” because it’s a substitute for its own training data in many cases.

OpenAI knows its killing referral traffic

OpenAI’s own media and economic experts attributed the drop in referral traffic for sites like the Times directly to AI summaries like Google’s AI Overviews. They’ve speculated that search referrals may be down as much as 60 percent.

Microsoft spokesperson Haurek cautioned that “Satya’s testimony and Microsoft’s position in this case are perfectly consistent. He spoke to broad principles and changes underway in how people find and consume information. Those observations should not be confused with conclusions about copyright questions before the Court, which Microsoft addresses in its filings.”

But it seems pretty clear based on this newly unsealed document that both Microsoft and OpenAI knew they were going to irreparably harm the publishing industry, the “millions of people” it employs, and, by extension, damage their own product, but carried forward anyway in pursuit of “gazillions” of dollars — doom loop be damned.
